title: Breathing and Healing in Africa, Part 1
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett shares their 25-year journey as a Zen practitioner, highlighting the importance of community, simplicity, and being open to new experiences. They reflect on how meditation practice can help cultivate awareness, presence, and curiosity about oneself and the world, allowing us to respond to suffering in a more compassionate way. By embracing simplicity and letting go of complex thoughts and judgments, we can deepen our understanding of ourselves and others, and find greater connection and meaning in life.

sentences.text: Good evening everybody.
Our way of practice is inherited from Japan.
We've messed around with it a lot, but it came from Japan.
I had a funny thought on the way to the forum.
I was just realizing on the way to the service that the Japanese are really big on anniversaries.
I think they used kind of decimal, base 10 anniversaries like us.
I remember a bunch of our colleagues went to Japan for the 850th anniversary of Dogen's death.
I was thinking that recent archaeological evidence from my files suggests that conversations that I had with Bob Penny and Florence Caplow to begin our sangha.
Before, I used to think that all happened in 1991, but now I think it happened in the winter of 1992, so therefore the winter of 2017, I think that's 25 years, right?
So we better have a party.
Which also means that the time that we celebrated our 20th anniversary was actually our 21st or 19th or something.
So, I don't know, when I encountered practice as a young man, I didn't have some big aha experience or didn't totally fix everything up.
But I just felt something, some connection or some feeling or touching something that I hadn't really felt before.
I didn't really have a good reason for why I wanted to continue doing meditation or continuing doing Zen.
I remember I had the idea that it was kind of like just trying it on, you know, like trying on a suit of clothes to see if it fits.
And there was no evidence yet that it didn't fit, but I didn't really know if it did fit.
So, anyway, 29 years later I feel kind of the same.
So it seems like it doesn't not fit.
So we might as well keep going.
I worked a little bit too long this afternoon.
I was doing some house repair work and it got to be like uncomfortably close to seven o'clock.
And it's so funny how grouchy the mind gets when I wanted, I had taken off my watch because I was painting, so I didn't really know what time it was.
And I was a little bit doing the thing, maybe you do this too, of trying to pretend that time was not passing.
And so when I came in, I think my mind actually did know that it was probably 6:20, 6:30, but my mind wanted it to be like 5:45, and it wasn't 5:45.
And I got so angry, you know, and I didn't want to come to practice.
But yeah, it seems like it's better to just keep coming.
So I came anyway.
And I'm glad I did.
So, I don't know if this is a very good testimonial for those of you who are new.
So it's like a kind of okay, sort of helpful thing to do, and I guess we should just keep going.
But you know, what else are we going to do, you know?
I mean, what really does help, right?
I mean, most of our ideas about what helps us, what we want help with, helps us feel happier or more satisfied or less upset or something like that.
We actually pay attention, most of those things don't really work anyway, right?
So it's pretty good to have something that probably sort of works consistently.
So anyway, it's really nice to be back in another way, not just that I got here tonight, but I was gone for most of July.

After, I don't know, 20 odd of those years of being here all the time, somebody smartly suggested to me, probably they'd been saying that for a long time and I finally heard it, that it would be good to take a little time off each year.
So I usually take July off as a little sabbatical.
And I really appreciate while I was gone, you know, many of you were here.
Sounds like things just kept rolling wonderfully, as one would think.
And it's great also that Ryushin Andrea, our newly transplanted Zen teacher in our sangha, gave a series of talks on the embodied nature of our practice.
And I understand she used some wonderful examples of a woman ancestors whose stories are being told a little more now.
When I started practice in the mid-80s, they had just recently renamed the list of the traditional list of people from the patriarch's list to the ancestors list.
So it was probably the patriarch's that we started.
It is all men, you know, on the so-called ancestors list.
Lately, we're remembering and learning and telling the stories of inspiring women, you know, who are probably the main reason why this practice kept going.
And so I haven't had a chance yet to listen to Andrea's talks.
Andrea, not Andrea's talks.
And I understand three were recorded and are already on the website thanks to Thales.
So if you weren't here either, let's set our intention to listen to those and appreciate her work and the conversations you had.
So as you might know, during this year's sabbatical, I actually took a big trip, a two-week trip to Kenya to meet and get to know an amazing young woman there.
Mercy Ukumu was a girl in a rural African village in western Kenya who was orphaned by AIDS.
Both her parents in quick succession died of AIDS when she was 12 years old.
She has an existing family.
She has actually five siblings and a couple of uncles and an aunt, maybe a second aunt that I didn't meet.

And so, you know, how would I even know about this person and how many people like this throughout the world are there that we don't know about, young people stuck one way or another by circumstances.
And at the time when she was 12 years old, not only did she have no parents, but there was no real source of income for the family.
Even though she's a second born, I don't know what was going on with her older brother, but somehow he wasn't able to function very well just then.
So she tried to support her family by doing things like reselling old clothes and making charcoal and selling charcoal.
And as you can imagine, probably not a very lucrative business in rural Kenya to sell charcoal or old clothes.
But anyway, it's a much longer story that I'll get into more later, but through a local friend here named Tim Costello, who used to sit with us in this very sangha, so it's all connected.
Through him, my wife and I got involved in sponsoring Mercy and helping her to live and study at a boarding high school.
And then she did so well at this high school, top marks, and pretty much everything depends on your high school grades.
Like, you know, we nag our kids here to get good grades, in two weeks, so I'm sure we'll be on his case.
But actually, if he gets an A or a B or a C in high school, he'll be fine, right?
He'll be fine.
But in Kenya, your marks completely determine whether you go to university.
Whether you're admitted, whether you're sponsored, with a little bit of government sponsorship there is.
So she got top marks, and she qualified for university and for a little bit of scholarship money from the government, but not near enough to live on and afford the schooling.
So Jan and I kept helping her.
At the time that we started helping her, our son was just leaving preschool.
So here we pay for our preschool, right?
We were both working, and we thought it would be good for him socially to go to preschool.
So that was something like two hundred fifty or three hundred a month.
I forget how much it was.

And when Tim came to us with this little folder with Mercy's twelve-year-old picture and some handwritten answers she'd made to questions, and told us that for eight hundred a year, we could completely support this girl, send her to a boarding high school, get her to a safe place, fed, you know, clothed, housed, and educated for eight hundred a year, we're like, geez, how do you not do that?
And several other young women in Kenya are now educated and mostly doing really well, thanks to other Bellingham families and Tim Costello's fearless initiative in setting this up.
One can imagine sort of having the opportunity to set something like this up.
Maybe you have had the opportunity maybe to set something like this up, but somehow Tim did it.

And so after all these years, nine years of sending money to the other side of the planet, you know, with bank transfers, and then the Dodd-Frank Act made that impossible, and then Western Union and other weird things, I finally got to meet her.
First thing I found out is we'd been saying her name wrong.

So it's interesting to be this connected to somebody, this big a part of their life, and I don't even know how to say their name, that M-E-R-C-Y, the word Mercy, a Christian name, as most of the names are in Kenya, is pronounced Mar-see in Kenyan English.
Not Mercy, Mar-see.
And I was there when she introduced herself to an American woman who just didn't get it.
It was kind of somewhere between Mercy and Mar-see, and she's like, Mercy?
Mar-see?
What?
And I said to her, well, if we looked at it, it would be spelled Mercy.
Then she called her Mercy the whole time.
So it's interesting, limits of language and pronunciation.

So to say that this was touching and heartwarming, finally meeting her, seeing her village being served food in the family compound and being accepted and welcomed, you know, really as a part of the family, I didn't feel like they were putting on a show for me to show their gratitude.
No, it was really like welcome home.
So this was really moving intensely.
So, and also really bewildering.
And I was thinking about how compassion is so confusing, you know?
And I think to practice compassion, this is what I'm realizing, to practice compassion, we have to be willing to be pretty confused and not sure what's going on.
Because how could this setup even be that we have so much and they have so little?
So I'm going to try to organize some of my pictures and show you some pictures next week if I can get it together.
So I'll just say a few things more about what happened and more next week.
But one example would be that the family, her family is basically doing fine.
Things are stable.
It's not a bad situation.
Security is okay where they are, like they're not worried for their safety.
They have little houses, a little compound, a little teeny two-room houses, square houses with two rooms.
And they have land for a small farm.
So that's pretty good.
They're okay.
And yet it's all so tenuous, you know?
So close to the edge.
Marcy's older brother Wellington is the farmer in the family.
And so he was showing me with a lot of pride the different fields that he has and the ones that he rents.
We went walking around the neighborhood, you know, to see his farms.
And he showed me down below the little creek there's a wet field that's, you know, wet most of the year and he's learned how to grow rice, which is recent in the region.
I don't know how long rice has been in Africa.
I would serve rice at every meal, so it's certainly well established.
And he showed me the fields that he was soon going to plow with rented oxen and his plow, you know, oxen-drawn plow, and weeded with one of his two hoes.
And this turned out to be one hundred percent of his farming equipment.
And he showed me the nursery bed with the little rice seedlings under mulch, beautiful little green, little sprouts.
So that was all good.
Then he showed me up the slope a little bit there was a cornfield, which is another very common crop, important crop there for eating in its store as well, right?
And also for cash.
And that this field was a dry field, no irrigation there, and so completely dependent on the rain, dry land farming.
But the rains, the big rains of April and May and into June had been much less than usual.
And so the corn hadn't done well anywhere.
And he showed us just these little kind of tiny ears and not too many of them.
And so the corn didn't produce as much, so less corn means less money.
And less money means they don't quite have school fees to send Marcy and Wellington's youngest sister, Sonia, to school.
So Sonia's hanging around at home helping out.
She's volunteering at her primary school because she wants to be a teacher one day, but she can't go to high school.
Not yet.
I forgot to ask how much the school fees were, but probably not, wouldn't sound like much to us.

It's strange, isn't it, you know, that the chain of karma and circumstance would be that way, that there is a place in the world with people whom I know and love where no rain means less cash, less cash means no school, no school means lives, at best are slipping by, and at worst young girls get pregnant, or worse.

When Marcy was destitute at twelve, I learned on this trip that a local police officer approached her in the hospital where she was caring for her dying father and offered to make her his fourth wife.
And she had enough self-understanding and drive.
She was a strong kid.
She knew this would be very bad, that she wouldn't go anywhere in her life, that she would more or less be a slave in his kitchens and in his bed.
So she decided she wouldn't have anything to do with men.
She made a vow in that moment not to have anything to do with men.
So, smart.
And here we are.
Our concerns are real enough.
Our suffering is real enough.
And I have the honor of getting to speak with many of you about your concerns and challenges.
It's hard to be a person.
I have to start another mindfulness class on Monday, and half the people in the group have serious clinical depression, anxiety, hospitalizations, big problems.
We are suffering, too.
And yet we are so well off.
I looked up some poverty statistics.
I will put the link to this on the website.
Eighty percent of people on the planet live on less than ten dollars a day.
Eighty percent of people.
So how would we do with three hundred bucks a month?
We have motorcycles, too.
They have motorcycles, too, actually.
One of the great ways to get around is motorcycle taxis.
They are really cheap.
Is it safe?
I don't know.
You can flag them down in any corner, and the standard fare is fifty shillings, which is about fifty cents.
In that context, Mercy Marcy can easily live on her salary.
Now that she is a successful woman with a job in the big city, she makes about four hundred fifty dollars a month.
The rent in her apartment is about one hundred twenty dollars.
So that is pretty good.
But she sends home all of her spare shillings to help her siblings, so it is actually not enough.
I was telling John a minute ago, and I am sure you have, too, we all have experienced difficulty financially.
All of us are in different situations.
There are funny little societal taboos about talking about our differences financially.
We have probably all seen poor areas in the States or other countries.

I have walked around very poor towns in Mexico and felt badly about it, but it was surprisingly a completely different thing to be inside the house, to be inside the family, to be receiving food that they grew and made themselves.
It was a totally different feeling.
So it is really worth thinking about our next purchase.
Not that we do not need to buy things, and we should buy what we need, and we should have a little fun, but what do we really need?
My feelings are shifting, I think, a little bit.
But habits are powerful.
I have noticed in the last five years in me, especially in the age of Amazon.com click and you are done, it is just so darn easy, isn't it?
Oh, I will just buy one.
It is so easy to do.
Maybe you are more restrained than I have been lately.
I had an interesting experience on Monday night, no, Sunday night, at Home Depot.
We recently had some work done on our house.
Janet, my wife, is really excited about a kitchen remodel.
So preparatory to that, there was some work happening in the stairwell next to the kitchen, which involved moving a window.

When the carpenters cut through to move this window, since the house is from nineteen oh three, an old house, they discovered that all the siding and the south face of the house had failed and had to be replaced.
So that goes half the kitchen budget.
That is upsetting.
They put in the new windows and the new siding, and to save a little money, I am going to do some of the painting.
I was trying to paint the window trim, all the window trim, and there was rot in there, so I had to replace all the window trim on the outside of the house.
It is a two-story house, and my tallest ladder, I could not quite safely reach the window upstairs.
I did all the other windows, and I really wanted to finish the job.
That feeling that really bothered me that I could not get to this upper window's trim.
My ladder was on a Sunday, so Home Depot is closed.
I am sorry, However Sales is closed, which is where I would have first gone to try to get some solutions.
So I go to Home Depot and I go to the ladder aisle thinking, I will just buy a ladder.
I have a tall house, I deserve to have a good ladder.
I will use it.
Of course, we have lived there for almost twenty years, and this is the first time that I have suddenly needed this taller ladder.
I have a twenty-two-foot extension ladder.
It is pretty big, but I need twenty-eight for this one part of the house.
So I go there thinking, I am saving money doing the work myself.
Maybe it will be one hundred dollars.
That will be okay.
I go to the ladder aisle and the ladder I need is two hundred eighty dollars.
I am like, oh.
I spent about fifteen minutes kind of walking up and down the ladder aisle and getting to the next aisle and going back and trying to decide what to do.
Luckily, nobody asked me if they could help me; they just left me alone.
So finally, I succumbed to convenience and I put the giant ladder on the giant cart and I am trying to move it around the aisle.
Even the wide aisles of Home Depot, it is pretty difficult to move a twenty-eight-foot ladder.
It is actually fourteen or fifteen feet long, like an extension.
So I get to the checkout counter, determined to buy my ladder and finish my job tonight, if possible.
It is like five o'clock, and I am probably hungry too.
The guy in front of me in line looks at my ladder, and there are two people in front of me, and the guy at the very front has some kind of problem, so it is going very slowly.
I am getting impatient too; I am just trying to get my damn ladder.
Things slow down a little bit.
We are waiting there for a while.
I calm down a little bit.
Then the guy in front of me, the middle guy, turns around, sees this enormous ladder on the cart, and says, "Hey, how much is that ladder?"
I do not know why he even asked me that.
I embarrassedly said, "Oh, it is almost three hundred dollars."
And he says to me, "Oh, I got one of those at home, just sitting around."
And he turns back the other way.
I do not know how much of a conscious thought process I had, but Americans do not ask strangers for help; that is not allowed.
But somehow I did.
I said, "Hey, could I borrow your ladder?"
And he said, "Sure.
Follow me home."
I did.
His name is Dennis, my new friend Dennis.
He saved me from spending three hundred dollars on a ladder, that is more with tax, right?

When Wellington in Kenya was telling me that he had no way of irrigating his cornfield, even though the stream is right down below, but no pump, no hoses, no way of doing that, he explained that the diesel pump that he wishes he could buy cost fifty thousand shillings.
That is completely out of reach.
It took me a while.
I was there to get the currency conversion straight, like being off by a factor of ten one way or the other.
One point, I went to the ATM and I took out what I thought was two hundred dollars, but it was actually twenty dollars, and it was very quickly gone.
I am like, "What happened to my two hundred dollars?"
It is actually twenty dollars.
So eventually I figured out that the fifty thousand shillings is five hundred dollars.
That is preventing him from having this whole other level of ability to grow food and take care of his family.

Here, if it were not for Dennis, I would have blown three hundred dollars on the ladder I did not really need, just because of impatience and a habit and wanting to be able to do it all myself, I guess.
So if we are vowing to save all beings, are we also vowing to think about all this stuff, to figure out about our own use of resources and money?
Are we vowing to understand our place in the world?
Are we vowing to be generous?
Generosity is the first of the six core practices of the Bodhisattva.
That is like our ideal, the Bodhisattva, the being that helps others awaken with awakens.
Should I send my three hundred dollars, my thirty thousand shillings, to Wellington for the pump?
I really do not know.
But I am really so grateful to have seen for myself what is like in rural western Kenya in the land of the Luo people.
I even know that was the name of them; they are the Luo.
There are forty-five tribes in Kenya with different languages, some of which are a little bit intelligible to each other, but most are not.
They live there, and have lived for I do not know how long.
They are interesting, too, just thinking about being in a place where human beings have lived since the beginning of human beings for a million years.
So it is truly our home.
People back home are struggling, is what I found out.
So perspective is really strange, isn't it?
When it shifts, it shifts.
One minute we look at things one way, the next minute we look at things a different way.
The whole world is different when our perspective shifts, our world changes.
Because our world is what we perceive it to be, right?
Of course, I knew in my head these statistics, and as I mentioned, I have seen poor villages in other places, I have been to the third world, but somehow this is different.
I am in it in a different way.
Our meditation practice turns on ethics, which is the next of these six practices of the Bodhisattvas, to be ethical.
Ethics supports our meditation practice.
How is it going?
How is our practice going?
Are we practicing?
Are we ethical?
Are we grounding ourselves in meditation?

I actually believe this is true that while meditation, while zazen, does not exactly give us some special insight or new something or other, like I was saying before, I think it is an important factor that allows for change, that invites space and flexibility in the mind.
When circumstances are such that we receive new information, feel new information, meditation helps us to be more available to that moment.

I do not know how many moments we miss, a lot, but maybe we miss fewer of them because of practice, because of spending some time regularly stopping, breathing, being curious about the space in between our solid ideas of who we are and who they are and how it is all going.
Noticing the little gaps, the cracks in the bell where the light gets through, like Leonard Cohen says, sings.

When we can just be with our thoughts without chasing them too much, without identifying with them too much, that simple thing that we did this evening, even if it was frustrating, even if we thought we were not doing it very well, if we spent most of the time spacing out or planning what we are doing tomorrow, any moment of deliberate, mindful engagement with our mind helps with this space, this allowing there to be more room for new thoughts, new patterns, new ways of thinking.
And that is what they mean when they say insight, when they say realization, something new emerges.
And then maybe there is a possibility of a new way of responding to suffering, a new way of helping.
How wonderful our awareness of breathing practice is.
We can get our head all tangled up, as I have proceeded to do here in my little talk.
I hope it is not too entangling to think about all this.
We are running around all day getting all tangled up in our mind, right?
But how great it is that we have this option to just feel our breathing, to feel the breathing in the body, to give the mind this healthy alternative.

If they had the diet diagrams, this much of this food and that much of that food that they are constantly changing as the milk lobby spends more or less money and stuff like that, what would that diagram be for how to use our mind, a healthy way to use our mind?
The mental food pyramid would probably not be totally filled in with obsessive thought and planning, right?
That should just be one little part of it.

How great that we can bring our attention and our awareness to mindfulness of breathing as an alternative, as a method for gently pulling back from our compelling thought space, emotion space, worry space, into the now space of just being present, open and curious.
It is great to do this in little snippets during the day.
It is great to sit down at home or in the Zen Center for half an hour, twenty minutes, ten minutes.
I do not know if it matters how long.
Just doing it.
I have always felt like one of our biggest obstacles is that we are so addicted to complexity, and so we think that we are so complicated.
I suppose we are.
We want to come to that conclusion based on all evidence, right?
We are complicated.
And our problems are complicated, so all the solutions must be really complicated.
This breathing thing seems pretty simple, stupidly so.
That's why we start with breath counting, which is the most simple possible option.
When you first hear about it, breath counting might sound like a modern innovation, like they must have thought of that in the sixties because they were so wired or something.
But no, it turns out to be really ancient.
There are early Chinese Buddhist texts that extol breath counting, and probably Indian texts too.
As long as there has been language and then there has been a mind and thinking, there has also been counting.
To feel the feeling of the breathing in the belly with each exhalation, to just quietly, silently add a very light number—one, two, three, and so on.
Maybe we get to ten, and then we just go back to one.
Maybe more likely, we start thinking about something or other, or some random thing happens in the mind, or we get distracted by something, and then we just go back to one.
It's beautiful too, the way counting keeps us honest: am I on three or four?
Maybe five.
I bet it's five.
Okay, six.
No.
That would be back to one.
Hearing that it's about getting to ten causes a little problem for us right away because we want to be good; we want to do it right.
We are so complicated.
So here is another thing that we need to learn: how to do it right.
What are the methods?
What is the inspiration?
What book should I read?
How many trainings should I do?
How do I do this right?
If I am not doing it right, is it okay to admit that I am not doing it right?
Are you doing it right?
It would probably be better if we did not say counting to ten.
We should just call it returning to one.
The great thing about two and three is they help you to return to one.
I really recommend breath counting.
What I am trying to say, strangely enough, is that I actually believe that counting our breath will help us to save the world, or at least take care of the world a little bit.
It is a little arrogant to say save the world, isn't it?
Americans would say that, and we should not see counting as a beginning practice or a beginner practice, even though we often do mention it to new people.
I do not know if we consistently say it in the orientation here; it would be nice if we did if there is time.
But we should see that we have a variety of different practices, and counting is one of several.
It is best to see all of our practices as equally beginner practices—beautifully beginner practices—so that we can all be beginners and practice beginner's mind.
The first temple that Suzuki Roshi created in San Francisco, they call it the beginner's mind temple, where every practice done with a good spirit is complete.
It is beginning and advanced and intermediate and everywhere in between.
Does that ranking help us in any way?
Dogen wrote in *The Practice of Enlightenment of the Buddha Way*, "Meeting one thing is mastering it.
Doing one practice is practicing completely."
So just breath counting is complete.
Just count.
Just count.
I find breath counting really helpful when I get super agitated in daily life too, or like, anxious in the middle of the night.
I think I have told this story several times that I did get tired of breath counting.
That is what I was taught in the beginning.

Then sometime, I do not know, five or six or seven years into my practice, I was doing a training period at the monastery, Tassajara monastery, which is like the high holy place of our lineage family.
I got in my head that I should be doing something more interesting by now at this monastery where I have all this time.
You are there; it is like, I do not know how many—six, eight, ten periods of meditation a day in this kind of integrated schedule where you are just there, you are in it, there is nowhere else to go.
So I went to the teacher and I said something like, I am sick of breath counting.
I think I had a more elaborate way of saying it, like maybe it is a little stale or mechanical, or there may be some more efficacious ways to, I do not know.
And she said, "Oh, I felt that way one time.
And you know what I figured out to do?
Just start at ten and count backwards."
So I did that for another three or four or five years or something like that.
There is nothing wrong with breath counting.
But if breath counting gets mechanical or you really cannot stand it, then please come see me or one of the other teachers, and maybe we will recommend that you keep counting and just stay with it.
Or maybe we will have some impulse, or it is nice to do a quieter practice in counting.
Counting is nice because it gives the cognitive mind something to do, right?
Instead of thinking about all that stuff, one, two.
Strangely, you can think about all kinds of things and also do that.
Another way of practicing is to let go of the counting or to let the counting just gradually fade to silence, fade away into the stillness of the moment and just follow the breath.
Just let the feeling of breathing in the body, especially in the center of the body, the belly, so grounding, or wherever you can feel it.
Chest is fine.
Just let the feeling of breathing be the center of experience.
Mind wanders.
Course.
No surprise.
But can you just come back to the breathing without beating yourself up?
Even a little bit?
Beating ourselves up is subtle, right?
It is kind of, we do not have to go to a full-blown, "Oh, you are crappy at this," but we know what we mean when we say to ourselves, right?
We know what that means.
The Buddha told a great teaching story, a famous teaching story, of the two arrows that is applicable.
The first arrow is the pain and discomfort of life, and it can be small, little pains and discomfort and annoyances.
"Darn it, I am spacing out during zazen."
A little bit of suffering there.
The pain and discomfort of life can of course be much, much bigger than that.
Illness, loss, catastrophes of all kind are inevitable, and when these things happen, it is painful.
Buddhism is famous for being really honest about this: do not always think really negative about this stuff.
The Buddha said to the monks and nuns one time, "Life just shot you with an arrow.
You have to admit that hurts."
Otherwise, it is stupid, right?

But the thing is, even though that is inevitable, we conditioned beings have a tremendous propensity to whip out our own bow and arrow and turn it around and somehow shoot ourselves with a second arrow.
We so easily add more suffering to our suffering, multiplying it with our habits of mind, the ways we think about things—so habitual: "I should be better than this.
I should know how to meditate by now.
This should not be happening.
This is not fair.
Why did she say that?
Why did she have to get sick?
Why do I have to have this problem?"
One could bring up a political example right now, but I will not.
If you must shoot a second arrow at yourself during zazen, the beautiful thing is it is a powerful opportunity, a beautiful situation in which we can notice that.
We can actually notice that, right?
We can say a little twinge of discomfort in the body, or a little moment of the mind wandering, or big pain in the body, and then some reaction, right?
Some anger, some annoyance, some impatience, some self-talk, some criticism.
